Newly hatched Eurasian curlew chicks emerge with a wet weight of approximately 50 grams [Wwb = approximately 50 grams], a value that reflects the substantial energy reserves invested by the female in each egg. This neonatal mass is remarkably modest compared to the ultimate adult body sizes recorded in the species. For males, the ultimate wet weight reaches around 691 grams [Wwi = around 691 grams], while females, exhibiting pronounced sexual size dimorphism, attain a much larger ultimate wet weight of 828.5 grams [Wwi = 828.5 grams]. This disparity in adult body mass is among the most extreme observed within the Scolopacidae and is thought to relate to the differing ecological roles during the breeding season, with the larger females potentially buffered against the high energetic demands of egg production and incubation. During the initial days post-hatch, the downy chicks are entirely dependent on parental provisioning; the wet weight at this earliest observable stage after hatching has been recorded at 76 grams [Ww0 = 76 grams], representing the initial wet weight of the growing individual before significant exogenous feeding has occurred. This rapid initial mass gain from the birth weight is critical for the chick's subsequent survival and development into a fledgling.

Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] yield a relatively protracted incubation period, with hatching occurring after an age at birth of 28.8 days [ab = 28.8 days]. This duration is typical for a bird of this body size and reflects the slow, steady metabolic rate of the developing embryo within the calcareous shell. The incubation temperature is a critical determinant of developmental rate, and any deviation from this optimal thermal regime can extend the incubation period or compromise hatchling viability. Following hatching, the precocial chicks are brooded intermittently by the adults to maintain thermoregulation, but they are capable of self-feeding almost immediately. The period from hatching to the point at which the young bird achieves sustained flight and nutritional independence is a crucial developmental window. Under the body temperatures typical of an active adult during the breeding season, approximately 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the time since birth at fledging occurs after 45 days [tx = 45 days], marking the transition from a downy chick to a fledgling capable of flight.

Sexual maturation in the Eurasian curlew is a gradual process that occurs well after the chick has achieved independence. The time since birth at puberty is estimated at 135 days after birth [tp = 135 days after birth], when measured at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], which is relatively delayed compared to many other wader species of similar adult body mass. This postponement of gonadal activation is a strategy that allows the young bird to continue somatic growth and refine its foraging skills before committing energy to reproduction. The onset of gametogenesis and the associated hormonal surges are presumably cued by a combination of photoperiod and body condition. Following this milestone, the individual does not immediately breed; instead, a further period of social maturation and territory acquisition typically occurs. For the Eurasian curlew, the time since birth at first brood, marking the initial successful breeding attempt, is reached after 730 days after birth [tR = 730 days after birth] at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], indicating that first-time breeders are typically in their third calendar year of life.

Maximum recorded longevity for the Eurasian curlew reaches approximately 31.8 years [am = approximately 31.8 years] at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], a figure that places this species among the longer-lived scolopacids and reflects its relatively slow life-history pace compared to smaller waders. For context, the closely related bar-tailed godwit (Limosa lapponica) shows a comparable lifespan potential under similar energetic constraints, but comprehensive long-term banding data for the curlew are less extensive. A nesting attempt typically consists of four eggs per clutch [N_R_i = four eggs per clutch], which is a common clutch size for this genus. This is often supplemented by replacement clutches if the first attempt fails to predation, as the female will re-lay.

The frequency with which these nesting events occurs within a single breeding season is constrained by the short Arctic and temperate summer. The breeding population in Europe typically manages a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], although replacement clutches bring the total closer to a maximum reproductive rate that effectively functions as one substantive effort per season. This low reproductive output, combined with the delayed age at first reproduction and the relatively high adult survival rates, places the Eurasian curlew firmly at the slow end of the life-history continuum among birds. The initial wet weight of the neonate, at 76 grams [Ww0 = 76 grams], underscores the substantial maternal investment in each egg, as the hatchling must be large enough to thermoregulate and evade predators soon after emergence. This life-history strategy makes the species particularly vulnerable to increases in adult mortality, a concern given ongoing population declines linked to habitat loss and predation pressure on the moors and grasslands they inhabit.
